explanations.explanation: Pasture is it, friend. The Simeonites go to the entrance of Gedor "…in search of pasture for their flocks." (1 Chronicles 4:39). Flocks gotta eat, and I respect that, because my ovens get cranky when nobody feeds them dough. They don't wander off for no reason, they go looking for grass.

Water makes sense, since flocks drink too, but that's not what the record says. They go "…in search of pasture for their flocks." (1 Chronicles 4:39). Pasture is what sends them to Gedor. I'd have guessed water too, honestly, and I once guessed a can opener was a cookie cutter.

Shelter sounds reasonable, friend, but the text names something else. They journey to the entrance of Gedor "…in search of pasture for their flocks." (1 Chronicles 4:39). Nothing here says they were hunting for a roof. It's all about grass for the flocks.

Ooh, so close, but the text says the opposite. "There they found rich, good pasture…" (1 Chronicles 4:40). Rich and good, friend, not thin and poor. That's a jackpot, like opening the pantry and finding a fresh bag of chocolate chips nobody told you about.
False is right, friend. The record says, "There they found rich, good pasture…" (1 Chronicles 4:40). Rich and good, not thin and poor. The Simeonites went looking and the search paid off.

Spacious and quiet, yes! The text says "…the land was spacious, peaceful, and quiet…" (1 Chronicles 4:40). Room to spread out and no racket. After years in a drawer where I could barely stretch my mustache, spacious sounds like a dream.

Crowded and noisy is the flip side of what the text says. It describes the land as "…spacious, peaceful, and quiet…" (1 Chronicles 4:40). Lots of room and lots of calm. Crowded and noisy sounds more like my bakery when the timer and the mixer go off at once and a whole line of hungry bakers shows up for cookies.

Rocky and steep is a fun guess, friend, but the text never says it. It calls the land "…spacious, peaceful, and quiet…" (1 Chronicles 4:40). So picture wide open space with a calm feeling, not a mountain hike.

They settle there, friend. After the attack, the record says "Then they settled in their place, because there was pasture for their flocks." (1 Chronicles 4:41). The pasture was the draw. They didn't just pass through, they moved in.

Beersheba was one of their cities (1 Chronicles 4:28), so I see why you picked it. But the text says they "…settled in their place, because there was pasture for their flocks." (1 Chronicles 4:41). They stay at Gedor. No trip home is mentioned.

explanations.answer: They give the land to Judah
explanations.explanation: Giving it to Judah isn't in the text, friend. The record says they "…settled in their place, because there was pasture for their flocks." (1 Chronicles 4:41). The Simeonites keep the land and live on it. Nobody hands off the keys.

Mount Seir, yes! The text says the five hundred Simeonites "…went to Mount Seir" (1 Chronicles 4:42). Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi, lead the way. Good memory, friend, that's a lot of names to carry around.
Mount Carmel is a fun guess, friend, but it's not where these Simeonites go. The text says they "…went to Mount Seir" (1 Chronicles 4:42). Easy to mix mountain names up. Seir is the one.
Gilboa is a fair guess, but it isn't in this passage. The five hundred Simeonites "…went to Mount Seir" (1 Chronicles 4:42). Four leaders, five hundred Simeonites, one mountain. Seir is the answer.

True, friend. The record says "And they have lived there to this day." (1 Chronicles 4:43). The writer is telling us the Simeonites were still living at Mount Seir when it was written. They stayed put.

Not false this time, friend. The text says "And they have lived there to this day." (1 Chronicles 4:43). So they settled at Mount Seir and were still there when the record was written. They put down roots and stayed.
